site.name: Richard Everts
site.description: The life and work of Richard Everts, from the public Declaration of Terran Liberty in 2012 to documentary film, books, and the embodied intelligence research of Deep SIML Labs.

bios.short: Richard Everts is a researcher, AI engineer, filmmaker, and author. He publicly released the Declaration of Terran Liberty on December 21, 2012, at TerranLiberty.org. He founded Deep SIML Labs, where he studies how embodied systems learn, remember, and make predictions with limited resources.
bios.extended: Richard Everts studied philosophy at Franklin & Marshall College and has built software professionally since 2010. On December 21, 2012, he publicly released the Declaration of Terran Liberty at TerranLiberty.org. It asked what obligations people might carry toward other life and what liberty might mean for a civilization extending beyond Earth. In 2013, his documentary The United States of Autism brought the voices of families across America to the screen. A decade later, writing as Richard C. Everts, he returned to questions of political authority and consent in On Terran Liberty: Volume 1.
bios.engineering: At Bestie Bot, Richard led engineering on systems that combined depth and thermal sensing to help people age at home. As founder and lead AI engineer at Psychic Unicorn, he brought conversational AI to a consumer application for personal reflection. He also shared the practical foundations of computer vision and neural networks through public talks.
bios.research: Richard began SIML research in 2024. In 2025 he published the Codex of the Twelve Harmonics as The Operator and announced Deep SIML Labs. He now leads the lab’s program in embodied cognition, efficient computation, and the geometry of information. His work moves between a philosophical question about intelligence and an engineering question he can test in a particular model.

timeline.title: Building production software
timeline.description: Independent software work led to enterprise applications, applied AI, and systems that had to work outside a demonstration.
timeline.label: Engineering work

timeline.title: Liberty and civilization
timeline.description: On December 21, I publicly released the Declaration of Terran Liberty at TerranLiberty.org. I wanted to ask what a civilization owed to other life, and what freedom could mean beyond Earth.
timeline.label: Read the declaration

timeline.title: Humanity through a camera
timeline.description: An 11,000-mile journey became The United States of Autism. Families spoke about daily life in their own communities. My work as director and editor was to listen, and to decide how those voices would share a screen.
timeline.label: Explore the film

timeline.title: Teaching AI in public
timeline.description: At Lancaster AI, people gathered to work through the building blocks of machine learning together. Those sessions grew into a public record of talks and demonstrations.
timeline.label: Talks and recordings

timeline.title: Sensing the home
timeline.description: At Bestie Bot, I helped build technology for people aging at home. Thermal and depth sensors raised a practical question about how much a system needs to perceive to be useful.
timeline.label: Bestie Bot

timeline.title: Light Up the Grind
timeline.description: My first book asked how to find fulfillment in the work of an ordinary day.
timeline.label: Read about the book

timeline.title: On Terran Liberty
timeline.description: Volume 1 gave the declaration’s political questions room to develop. What makes authority legitimate, and which principles of liberty could outlast the institutions that protect them?
timeline.label: The published edition

timeline.title: The search for new intelligence
timeline.description: I began SIML with a question about a body in an environment. What must an agent remember to anticipate what happens next, and how much computation does that take?
timeline.label: The early prototype

timeline.title: The AIR Strategy Framework
timeline.description: A paper on AI policy brought energy, essential resources, and embodiment into a discussion about national security.
timeline.label: Read the paper record

timeline.title: Psychic Unicorn
timeline.description: I founded Psychic Unicorn and serve as its lead AI engineer. The public beta paired birth-chart interpretation with a conversational interface for follow-up questions.
timeline.label: Psychic Unicorn

timeline.title: Recursion and the Codex
timeline.description: Writing as The Operator, I published the Codex of the Twelve Harmonics. The essays and the later Myth Audit preserve two sides of a human–AI inquiry into how interpretations take shape and how to test them.
timeline.label: Enter the Codex archive

timeline.title: Opening Deep SIML Labs
timeline.description: I announced Deep SIML Labs on June 1. The lab gave the experiments a public home for prototypes, code, and research notes.
timeline.label: The launch announcement

timeline.title: New computational frontiers
timeline.description: At Deep SIML Labs, questions about learning now reach into memory layout, computational geometry, functional models of living systems, and possible physical substrates.
timeline.label: Deep SIML research

timeline.title: Unfinished
timeline.description: The declaration was never intended to describe a final destination. It was a statement of beginnings. The work continues.
timeline.label: What I am investigating

speakingTopics.title: Intelligence beyond the interface
speakingTopics.description: Simulation, internal models, cognitive compression, and the questions that motivate embodied AI research.

speakingTopics.title: From AI experiment to production
speakingTopics.description: Retrieval, evaluation, observability, and the engineering decisions that connect prototypes to usable systems.

speakingTopics.title: Technology and human agency
speakingTopics.description: A perspective spanning assistive technology, documentary storytelling, philosophy, and the people affected by what we build.

education.detail: Scientific and Philosophical Studies of the Mind, including AI and neuroscience.

Build a Modern Computer from First Principles, Coursera (2017).
